BULK RNA-SEQ : A FAIR APPROACH

rnaseq-flow

From FASTQ to differential expression, splicing, fusions and pathways, in one run that records how it got there.

Nicholas Owen · UCL Advanced Research Computing · version 1.9.1 · November 2026

Thanks for having me. I'm Nicholas, from ARC. This is rnaseq-flow, a bulk RNA-seq pipeline I've been building in Nextflow. It has changed a lot since I last showed it: it now goes from raw reads all the way to differential expression, splicing, transcript usage, fusions and enrichment in a single run, and every run leaves a record of what it did and who did it. The current release is 1.9.1, with its own Zenodo DOI. I'll cover what it is, how it works, and why it is worth using wherever you run your analysis: a laptop, a desktop, a cluster, the cloud or a TRE.

THE PROBLEM

Most RNA-seq runs stop at a count matrix

The data arrives as FASTQ. The question is biological.

A matrix and a QC report, with the biology still to do.

Expression, splicing and fusions as separate runs and samplesheets.

A stranded library read as unstranded: plausible, and wrong.

An analysis reaches a paper with nobody named for it.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

Most RNA-seq processing ends at a count matrix and a QC report, and that is not the question anyone asked. The widely used community pipeline, nf-core/rnaseq, says so itself: it produces a matrix and QC and does not assign significance. Differential expression, splicing and fusions are each a separate pipeline, with their own samplesheet and their own references, and every boundary is a chance for the annotation, the baseline or the sample labels to disagree. Some mistakes don't fail at all. A stranded library processed as unstranded gives splicing values that look entirely plausible and are wrong; rnaseq-flow itself had exactly that bug in rMATS until 1.9.0. And the analyst, often core facility staff, does the work that ends up in a paper without an author line or any machine-readable record.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

In one sentence: one samplesheet in, a whole analysis out. The input is a four-column CSV: sample, read 1, read 2 and condition. If you already have counts, from GEO or a collaborator, a count matrix can enter instead and skip straight to differential expression. Every tool runs in its own container, so the only things to install are Nextflow, Java and a container engine. What comes out is a results folder, a MultiQC report for QC and a Quarto report for the analysis, and a record: a run manifest, a Workflow Run RO-Crate, and a reproduce folder beside every analysis that draws figures. It is the downstream sibling of refdata-flow: same Nextflow style, same SGE profile.

HOW IT WORKS

Four stages, one command

01 · Clean

02 · Align or quantify

03 · Count and test

04 · Look further

Raw reads are profiled, then trimmed of adapters and low-quality bases.

FastQC · fastp

One of four aligners, chosen by one flag. Strandedness is inferred per sample.

STAR · HISAT2 · Salmon · Kallisto

One gene count matrix, tested by two independent callers in parallel.

featureCounts · tximport · DESeq2 · edgeR

Splicing, transcript usage, fusions and pathways, then one report over it all.

rMATS · DEXSeq · fgsea · Quarto

Stop early with --stop_at preQC | postQC | DE | GSEA; start late with --counts.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

Under the hood, four stages. FastQC profiles the raw reads and fastp trims them. Then one of four aligners: two genome aligners, STAR and HISAT2, or two pseudo-aligners, Salmon and Kallisto. On the genome routes RSeQC works out the strandedness of each sample and feeds it straight into featureCounts. Third, one gene count matrix, from featureCounts or from tximport, tested by DESeq2 with apeglm shrinkage and by edgeR's quasi-likelihood test, in parallel and independently, so genes both call are your most robust hits. Finally the analyses gene-level counts can't see: rMATS splicing events, edgeR diffSplice, DEXSeq transcript usage, isoform switching, STAR-Fusion, then GSEA and gProfiler, and one Quarto report over all of it. You can stop early for a quick QC pass, or start late from a count matrix.

ROUTES

Four aligners, one --aligner flag

AlignerKindUnlocks downstream
STARgenome · defaultfeatureCounts, RSeQC, bigWig, rMATS, exon diffSplice, STAR-Fusion
HISAT2genome · lighterthe same, without fusion calling
Salmonpseudo-alignertximport, DEXSeq DTU, transcript diffSplice, isoform switching
Kallistopseudo-alignertximport, DEXSeq DTU, transcript diffSplice

Every route ends in DESeq2, edgeR, GSEA and gProfiler. HISAT2 still gives counts: featureCounts runs after either genome aligner.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

You choose one aligner per run with one flag, and the downstream stages adapt to it. STAR is the default, and its sorted BAMs unlock the most: featureCounts, RSeQC, coverage tracks, rMATS, exon-level diffSplice and fusion calling. HISAT2 is the lower-memory genome route with the same downstream stack minus STAR-Fusion. Worth saying: on nf-core/rnaseq, HISAT2 gives you a BAM and no expression estimates; here featureCounts runs after either genome aligner, so HISAT2 is a lighter route to the same analysis, not a dead end. Salmon and Kallisto are the fast transcript-level routes, summarised to genes by tximport, and they unlock transcript usage; isoform switching is Salmon only. Since 1.8.0 the transcriptome they index is cut from the genome and GTF with gffread, so index and annotation describe the same transcripts by construction.

nf-core/rnaseq 3.27.0 is the stronger front half: more preprocessing, QC and testing. Compared from its documentation, 1 November 2026.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

This is the honest comparison with nf-core, which most people here will know. nf-core gives you four excellent specialist pipelines: rnaseq for QC and counts, differentialabundance for statistics and pathways, rnasplice and rnafusion. That means four runs, separate samplesheets, a contrasts file, and references to keep consistent between them. rnaseq-flow answers all of it in one run, from one samplesheet, with every analysis oriented against the same baseline. To be fair in the other direction: nf-core/rnaseq is the better front half. It has UMI handling, rRNA and contaminant removal, more QC tools and far more testing. Some of that is on my roadmap, and I'll come back to it. This comparison is from nf-core's own documentation; I haven't run it side by side.

WHY USE IT

What it gives researchers, wherever they run it

Mistakes refused at launch, figures that redraw, a record of who did what, and the same pipeline on any machine.

So far, what it is. Now why it is worth using. Four things: mistakes are refused before they cost a run, every figure can be redrawn from the results folder, every run records what it did and who did it, and the same pipeline runs on a laptop, a desktop, a cluster or the cloud. I'll finish this part with running where there is no network at all.

BENEFIT 1 · CORRECTNESS

Refused at launch, not after alignment

A baseline that exists

A --reference_level missing from the samplesheet stops the run, so no fold change silently inverts.

Names R can use

Values such as TGF-beta or 6h are refused with a replacement, before hours of alignment.

Skipped work says so

An analysis asked for that cannot run gives a reason, rather than a green run without it.

# every check a real run makes,

# then exit before any job

nextflow run main.nf \

  --input samplesheet.csv \

  --validate_only

Non-zero on failure, so it gates a submission script.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

First, correctness. A schema can check that a column exists; it can't check what the values mean. So before any process is scheduled the pipeline checks the things that otherwise fail after alignment and quantification have already run, or don't fail at all. The baseline condition decides which way every result points, so a reference level that isn't in the samplesheet stops the run rather than falling back to alphabetical order. Condition, batch and design covariate values have to be valid R names, because DESeq2 builds its coefficient names from them. It also needs two conditions with at least two replicates each, a container engine, and an organism that matches the reference. And since 1.9.0, an analysis you asked for that couldn't run is listed in the report with the reason. The validate-only flag runs all of this and exits, so it can sit in front of any job submission.

BENEFIT 2 · REPRODUCIBILITY

Every figure redraws from the results

A script per figure

Each analysis folder carries reproduce/: a commented R script, its tables, and only the objects it needs.

Settings at the top

Contrast, cutoffs, colours and size are named constants in the first lines. No ggplot chain to read.

No cluster required

A collaborator redraws months later without the pipeline, the references or the compute.

# in deseq2_output/reproduce/

Rscript volcano.R

 

# writes repro_* figures, each

# with an .info.txt of the

# settings that made it

SVG and PNG at 300 dpi; one pair of cutoffs, --padj_cutoff and --lfc_cutoff, shared by every table and figure.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

Second, reproducibility at the level people actually need it: the figure. A published figure that can't be adjusted is just a picture. Every analysis that draws something carries a reproduce folder with a standalone, commented R script per figure type, gzipped copies of the tables it reads, and the R objects a plot genuinely needs, always the smallest that will do. The settings worth changing are named constants in the first lines. It runs from a terminal or RStudio, and redrawn figures are prefixed repro and carry a note of the settings and environment. GSEA needs this most: its table plot reads gene-set membership from the GMT, which is never published with results, so without the folder that figure couldn't be redrawn at all. And since 1.9.0 one pair of significance thresholds is shared by DESeq2, edgeR, the gProfiler lists, the figures and the report, so they can't disagree.

BENEFIT 3 · PROVENANCE AND CREDIT

A results folder that explains itself

run_manifest.json

Version and commit, command line, aligner, baseline, thresholds, design and reference release.

RO-Crate

One action per task, a SHA-256 per published file, and the pipeline as it ran.

run_contributors

Each analyst as a Person with an ORCID, behind CRediT roles, with the project's RAiD.

Core facility staff run analyses that reach papers without an author line. The crate names them.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

Third, provenance, and this is the part I care most about as a data steward. It is on by default, because provenance that has to be remembered isn't provenance. The run manifest records how the run was configured: version and commit, the command line, the aligner, the baseline, the thresholds, the design, the samples per condition, and the reference set with its Ensembl release. The Workflow Run RO-Crate says the same in standard JSON-LD that WorkflowHub and other tools can read: one action per task with its inputs and outputs, a checksum for every published file, and the pipeline itself as it ran. And it records people. Each contributor is a Person with an ORCID behind CRediT roles as resolvable URIs, it says whether a role was stated or inferred from who launched the run, and the project carries a RAiD, funder, grant and rights holder. Identifiers are checked at launch. nf-core ships a crate describing its code; this one describes your run.

RUNS ANYWHERE

One pipeline, any machine

ProfileWhereWhat it does
dockerlaptop or desktopeach tool in its own container
singularityshared servers and HPCcontainers without a Docker daemon
condano container engineenvironments solved at run time
sgeSGE clustersmemory per core, local scratch, high-memory routing
slurmSlurm clustersany site, set by partition and account
treTREs and air-gapped systemsevery image from the offline bundle

Other schedulers and cloud batch services are Nextflow executors: copy conf/sge.config or pass a small -c config. Profiles combine, such as -profile test_yeast,docker.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

The same pipeline runs on a laptop, a desktop, a shared server, a cluster or the cloud; what changes is one profile. Docker is the usual choice on a laptop or workstation. Singularity or Apptainer is for shared infrastructure where Docker isn't available. Conda works with no container engine at all, slower, and it needs network access to solve environments. The SGE profile is tuned for SGE clusters: it requests memory per core the way SGE expects, rounded up, uses node-local scratch, and routes the one job that needs a high-memory node, a splice-aware HISAT2 index for human or mouse, to those nodes automatically. The TRE profile runs from the offline bundle, which is the next slide. For SLURM or another scheduler, or for a cloud batch service, Nextflow supplies the executor: copy the SGE config as a starting point or pass a few lines with -c. No cloud profile ships with the pipeline yet.

SENSITIVE DATA

Runs where there is no network

Every container, in one bundle

27 Singularity images, about 7 GB, with the provenance plugin and a tre.config.

Published, with a DOI

On Zenodo, so a TRE can take a citable, fixed copy through its own transfer route.

Same results, offline

Nothing is fetched at run time, and the RO-Crate is still written.

# inside a TRE or air-gapped cluster

export NXF_OFFLINE=true

nextflow run main.nf \

  -c $NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR/tre.config \

  -profile tre,sge ...

doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21880328

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

A lot of our RNA-seq is on human samples, and some of it has to live in a Trusted Research Environment. As configured, the pipeline can't run there: several containers are provisioned at run time by Nextflow's Wave service, which needs the internet. So there is a complete offline bundle on Zenodo: 27 Singularity images, about seven gigabytes, the nf-prov plugin that writes the RO-Crate, and a tre config that switches Wave off and pins every image locally. You download it outside, bring it in by whatever route your environment allows, and run with the tre profile, alone or with SGE. The bundle has its own DOI, separate from the pipeline's, and the v1.8.0 bundle is the one that works with the current release. References and gene sets need fetching outside first.

GETTING STARTED

Three commands from nothing to results

# 1 · references from Ensembl, pinned

nextflow run main.nf --download_refs \

  --download_species homo_sapiens ...

# 2 · the index for one aligner

nextflow run main.nf --build_indices \

  --aligner star --genome_fasta ... --gtf ...

# 3 · the analysis

nextflow run main.nf --input samplesheet.csv \

  --aligner star --star_index ... --gtf ... \

  -profile docker

Try it on yeast first

Six samples and a 12 Mb genome: all four aligners on a laptop.

Or bring refdata-flow

Pass the paths refgenie seek prints to --genome_fasta and --gtf.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

Getting started is three invocations of the same entry point. The first fetches a genome, annotation and gene sets from Ensembl, pinned to a release, with a metadata file recording where they came from. The second builds the index for your aligner, or all four at once. The third runs the analysis. If you've never used it, start with the yeast example: it fetches a six-sample dataset and walks through all four aligners, and a 12 megabase genome indexes in about two gigabytes, so it runs on a laptop with the test_yeast profile. And if you're already using refdata-flow, the two fit together: the genome and annotation are just paths, so you pass in what refgenie seek prints. One caveat there: the organism check reads a metadata file only rnaseq-flow's own download writes, so set the organism yourself.

rnaseq-flow · UCL ARC

Where are we? Everything on the left is released, as 1.9.1, with a concept DOI on Zenodo that resolves to every version. The checks that run in CI today are static: channel topology and process arity, the report's R code and the modules, plus a stub run that exercises both the genome and the pseudo-aligner routes and each of the launch refusals. What that doesn't prove is that a process produces what the next one expects, and that's where the last round of review found its problems. So next is per-process tests with nf-test, starting with the processes where a wrong answer is silent: rMATS, DESeq2, edgeR, tximport and featureCounts. Then the protocol gaps against nf-core, UMI handling and rRNA removal, because a UMI library processed without UMI handling gives wrong numbers. Then merging re-sequenced libraries, and later duplicate marking and deeper QC.
